title: Jamaican Folklore: Duppies, the Rolling Calf and Anansi Stories
metaDescription: Start with Jamaica’s duppy and Rolling Calf, then explore Anansi storytelling. Read source notes and distinguish Jamaican accounts from wider Caribbean traditions.
intro: A duppy is a spirit in Jamaican storytelling; the Rolling Calf is one frightening form in recorded accounts. Anansi belongs to a different kind of story, where wit and appetite often matter more than terror.

sections.title: Start with the ghost stories
sections.text: Martha Warren Beckwith’s Jamaica Anansi Stories (1924) includes a note describing the Rolling Calf as a duppy with fiery eyes. A spirit category and a particular apparition therefore need not be two unrelated species.

sections.title: Read Anansi as a storyteller’s character
sections.text: Beckwith’s collection records named tellers, locations, stories and songs. Its Anansi is a trickster within a storytelling tradition, not simply another hostile creature to defeat. The related Anansi entry below is filed under Ghana; the collection linked here supplies the Jamaican context.

sections.title: Keep the island and the source in view
sections.text: Caribbean traditions travel, but a name recorded on another island is not automatically a Jamaican origin story. The list below focuses on Duppy and Rolling Calf. The 1924 collection is a historical record mediated by its collector, not a claim that every Jamaican tells the same stories today.

questions.question: Is a Rolling Calf a duppy?
questions.answer: Beckwith’s collection explicitly describes the Rolling Calf as a duppy. That relationship is the starting point used here.

questions.question: Are all Caribbean creatures Jamaican?
questions.answer: No. Follow the location and collector attached to each account; a regional name alone does not establish its origin.
